title: Is your OT environment ready for what comes next?
summary: Discover why AI and OT automation readiness both begin with a resilient OT foundation that can support production, manage complexity and adapt to demands.
body_markdown:
Most plants weren’t designed for the connectivity and data exchange AI needs. As a result, longstanding OT weaknesses are being exposed after they’ve accumulated across decades.


Now we’re asking these environments to move more data, connect more systems, support more applications and provide a secure foundation for AI-enabled manufacturing. That means the OT environment must be able to **absorb new demands without putting production at risk** .


## Five realities reshaping the meaning of OT resilience


Years ago, few manufacturers could’ve predicted how quickly AI-enabled applications would become an operational priority—or the new demands they would place on OT environments.


There’s no way to know what the next major demand for your plant might look like. It could involve a new production application, an acquisition or another technology that has yet to emerge.


To me, planning for **this uncertainty is what operational resilience is all about** : building an OT environment that can support production while adapting to what comes next. Deploying reliable switches, redundant networks or a good[cybersecurity program](https://www.belden.com/blog/improving-warehouse-efficiency-depends-on-secure-connections) is part of the equation, of course, but it isn’t the whole story.


The challenge is building and maintaining that resilience in an environment that’s more connected and more difficult to manage than it used to be.


These are the five realities I tell manufacturers they need to understand and prepare for if they want to **build an OT environment that can keep up with AI and whatever else comes next** .


### 1. Production has more dependencies than it used to


The more connected manufacturing becomes, the more infrastructure reliability becomes production reliability. In a highly siloed plant, a failure might stay relatively contained. That’s becoming less true in[connected environments](https://solutions.belden.com/warehousing-logistics-newsletter) where production depends on systems, applications and people being able to communicate. This is why I tell manufacturers to consider resilience beyond the individual layer, thinking about how a disruption in one system could affect the systems, people and processes around it.


A network issue can now affect an HMI, interrupt communications, prevent data from reaching an MES or delay someone’s ability to understand a quality problem. Suddenly, the network problem becomes a production problem—and production problems turn into business problems. Delayed schedules, labor inefficiencies, late orders, material issues and missed customer commitments can follow.


This is even more important in multi-site manufacturing, where a disruption at one facility can affect production planning at another.
